parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=(x+1)e^{1-x}$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, points of inflection, intercepts and showing what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.

solutions.latex:
$f'(a)=0$, so $x=a$ is a stationary point.

$f''(a)=\pi>0$, so the curve is concave up there.

Therefore $x=a$ is a local minimum turning point.

Answer: B

Let $u=\sin x$, $u'=\cos x$, $v=\ln x$, $v'=\dfrac{1}{x}$.

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[(\sin x)(\ln x)\big]=u'v+uv'=(\cos x)(\ln x)+\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$$

Answer: D

For concave down, $f''(x)<0$.

$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2+2x\\f''(x)&=6x+2\end{aligned}$$

$6x+2<0\Rightarrow x<-\dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: B

Translate left by $\pi$: $\ln x\to\ln(x+\pi)$.

Dilate horizontally by scale factor 3: replace $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{3}$, giving $y=\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi\right)$.

Answer: A

$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=e^{t}-e^{-t}\\x'(t)&=e^{t}+e^{-t}\\x''(t)&=e^{t}-e^{-t}=x(t)\end{aligned}$$

Answer: C

$f'(x)<0$ where the curve is decreasing: to the left of the minimum at $(-4,-2)$ and to the right of the maximum at $(2,2)$.

So $x<-4$ or $x>2$.

Answer: B

$y=\log_2 x$ is shifted left by 3 and down by 2.

The point $(1,0)$ moves to $(-2,0)$ and then to $(-2,-2)$; the vertical asymptote becomes $x=-3$.

Only graph D is increasing with asymptote $x=-3$ and passes through $(-2,-2)$.

Amplitude $=\dfrac{8-2}{2}=3$, so $a=3$.

Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}=\pi$, so $b=2$.

Answer: C

$$y=-\left(\sqrt{5}(x+8)\right)^2+7$$

Either order of description is accepted:

\textbf{Method I}

1. Horizontally translated to the left by 8.

2. Vertically reflected about the $x$-axis and dilated by scale factor 5.

3. Translated up by 7.

\textbf{Method II}

1. Horizontally dilated by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

2. Horizontally shifted to the left by 8.

3. Vertically reflected about the $x$-axis.

4. Vertically shifted up by 7.

solutions.latex:
$-\pi\le x\le\pi\Rightarrow-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$

Reference acute angle: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; $\tan$ is positive in quadrants 1 and 3.

$$\begin{aligned}x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\&=-\dfrac{4\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{6}\\&=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\sin x$$

$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore m_{\text{normal}}=\sqrt{2}$, and using the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$:

Equation of normal:

solutions.latex:
For stationary points $f'(x)=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3-3x^2=0\\x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$

When $x=-1$: $y=1+3\times(-1)-(-1)^3=1-3+1=-1$, so the point is $(-1,-1)$.

When $x=1$: $y=1+3\times1-(1)^3=1+3-1=3$, so the point is $(1,3)$.

$$f''(x)=-6x$$

When $x=-1$: $f''(-1)=-6\times(-1)=6>0$, concave up, $\therefore(-1,-1)$ is a local minimum turning point.

When $x=1$: $f''(1)=-6\times1=-6<0$, concave down, $\therefore(1,3)$ is a local maximum turning point.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: any one point with both x and y coordinates; 1: nature of (-1,-1); 1: nature of (1,3) (or use of f'(x) for neighbourhood testing around x = -1 and x = 1)

solutions.latex:
Possible point of inflection occurs when $f''(x)=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}-6x&=0\\x&=0\\y&=1+3\times0-0^3=1\end{aligned}$$

so the point is $(0,1)$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-0.1&0&0.1\\\hline f''(x)&0.6>0&&-0.6<0\\\hline&\cup&&\cap\end{array}$$

Since the concavity changes, $\therefore(0,1)$ is a point of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Maximum area may occur when $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta&=0\\10\sin\theta&=5\cos\theta\\\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\\tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

With $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (right triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$), $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\\&=-5\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-10\cos\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=-5\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-10\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}<0\end{aligned}$$

concave down, $\therefore\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives maximum area.

solutions.latex:
$y$-int: $y=e^{1}=e$

$x$-int: $0=(x+1)e^{1-x}$, $(x+1)=0$ as $e^{1-x}\ne0$, $x=-1$

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{1-x}+(x+1)e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\&=e^{1-x}(1-x-1)\\&=-xe^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$

For stationary points: $x=0$, $y=e$

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-1\times e^{1-x}-x\times e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\&=e^{1-x}(-1+x)\end{aligned}$$

When $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\times e^{1}<0$, concave down.

$\therefore x=0$, $y=e$ gives a local max. turning point.

For points of inflection: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0\Rightarrow x=1$, $y=2\times e^{0}=2$, i.e. $(1,2)$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0.9&1&1.1\\\hline\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&-0.11<0&&0.09>0\\\hline&\cap&&\cup\end{array}$$

Since the concavity changes, $\therefore(1,2)$ is a point of inflection.

As $x\to+\infty$: $x+1\to+\infty$, $e^{1-x}\to e^{-\infty}\to\dfrac{1}{\infty}\to0$, $\therefore y\to0$

As $x\to-\infty$: $x+1\to-\infty$, $e^{1-x}\to e^{\infty}\to\infty$, $\therefore y\to-\infty$
